description: We are students from MoAI (student club from Lublin University of Technology). We thrive in space themed hackathons.
summary: Astrobalance is offline health-monitoring software that lets astronauts check their own health on long missions, where there is no doctor on board and a message to Earth takes up to about 22 minutes one way. After a two-minute daily check-in (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood and a reaction test), an unsupervised model learns each astronaut's personal normal and turns the last two weeks into one Systemic Anomaly Index from 0 to 100, with a clear status (Watch or Act), the values that moved and the next step. Fixed critical limits and a step-by-step emergency guide work independently of the model from day 1. In a one-time test on an illness type the model never saw (infection onset), it caught 10 of 10 cases, a median of 5 days earlier than fixed clinical limits, with 4.4 times fewer false alarms than single-value limits; on real everyday data from 16 people it raised no alarm in 280 person-weeks. Every NASA Human Research Program hazard is visible in the app, and the same approach can serve isolated crews on Earth, such as Antarctic stations and remote communities. Proof of concept on synthetic data calibrated on published sources; not a medical device.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Astrobalance is an offline app that lets astronauts assess their own health on long missions, where there is no doctor on board and a message to Earth takes up to about 22 minutes one way. It works on two paths.

• Prevent. A two-minute guided daily check-in (blood pressure, resting heart rate, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood and a reaction test) is compared with the astronaut's own normal, learned in the first 21 mission days and then slowly updated. A personal-drift model (Mahalanobis / Hotelling T² distance of the 14-day weighted mean of personal deviations, learned without any illness labels) turns this into one Systemic Anomaly Index from 0 to 100. The crew sees Watch or Act, which values moved, and up to three next steps.

• Respond. Fixed critical limits raise a red alert without the model, and an emergency guide for a crew mate (unresponsive, CPR, chest pain, breathing difficulty), adapted to microgravity, is always one tap away. Escalation follows the signal delay: the crew medical officer first, then one structured SBAR report queued for Earth; a blackout mode covers Mars solar conjunction.

What benefits does it have?

• Earlier warning: in a one-time test on an illness type the model never saw (infection onset) it caught 10 of 10 cases, a median of 5 days earlier than fixed clinical limits.

• Alerts a crew can trust: 0.055 false alarms per crew member per week (clinical limits 0.121, single-value limits 0.241), and no alarm in 280 person-weeks of real everyday data (PMData, 16 people).

• Explainable: every alert says which values moved and what to do next.

• Works without Earth: fully offline and installable, no account and no server.

• A safety net from day 1 that does not depend on the model.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Crews on Moon and Mars missions get a tool to notice slow health changes early and act on board, when Earth cannot answer in time, with all five NASA Human Research Program hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity, closed environment) visible in one place. On Earth the same approach serves isolated crews and communities: Antarctic stations in winter, remote communities with little access to care (the use named by the challenge author) and long voyages at sea. A personal normal needs no patient database and no constant connection.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

• Python 3.11 (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch for the benchmarked autoencoders, Matplotlib, PyYAML, Requests, jsonschema, pytest) for simulation, modelling and evaluation.

• JavaScript with React 18, Vite 6 and Tailwind CSS 4 for the web app, installable and offline through our own service worker.

• NASA APIs and data: DONKI solar particle events, JPL Horizons ephemeris, NASA OSDR (Inspiration4).

• GitHub Actions (72 automated tests on Linux and Windows) and GitHub Pages for hosting.

• No special hardware: a phone, tablet or laptop plus standard devices (blood pressure cuff, thermometer, glucose meter); the reaction test runs on the screen.

• All code is open source under Apache-2.0.

How is your project creative?

• Each astronaut is compared with themselves, and all values are watched together: the model warns when several small changes add up, before any single value crosses a limit.

• "Is it me or the habitat?": when the same body system drifts in two or more crew members, the app points to the cabin first (CO₂, food or water, schedule, an infection, a solar event) instead of one person. Crewmates are counted, never named.

• "Feels fine is not always fine": before a spacewalk, docking or robotic-arm work, the app compares how astronauts rate their mood with their reaction test, because tiredness hides from one's own judgement (Van Dongen et al. 2003).

• Real distance in the interface: for a crew on Mars the app shows the true one-way delay of that mission day from NASA/JPL Horizons, not a fixed number.

• We tested the idea like an experiment: the model was chosen in a fair benchmark of 42 configurations (it beat deep-learning autoencoders), thresholds were frozen, and one illness type was held out and evaluated once; the evaluation script refuses a second run and the tests check it.

• One visual language for every state: each status has its own colour, shape and word, so it reads at a glance, even for colour-blind users and readers whose first language is not English.

What factors did your team consider?

• Distance and blackouts: any answer from Earth takes a round trip of up to about 44 minutes, and contact stops for about two weeks during solar conjunction, so every step works on board first and reports wait in a queue.

• The crew medical officer may be the one who is ill: the guidance is written for any crew member.

• Alarm fatigue: every method was held to the same false-alarm budget, and a status change needs 3 days in a row, so the crew keeps trusting the alerts.

• Safety: critical limits and the emergency guide never depend on the model.

• Use in space: large tap targets (64 px) for gloves, a two-minute guided check-in, a colour-blind-safe palette with shapes and words.

• Privacy: check-ins stay on the device, and crewmates' health appears only as counts.

• Scientific honesty: astronaut health records are private, so the crews are synthetic, calibrated on published sources and checked against real data (PMData and Inspiration4 blood tests from NASA OSDR); every assumption is listed in the README. Proof of concept, not clinical validation and not a medical device.

• Open, reusable work: open licenses, every source cited, no NASA branding.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used Claude (Anthropic), including through Claude Code, as a coding and writing assistant: it drafted Python code, tests, configuration, the web app's code and texts, figures, the README, the demo slides and helped us search for and check sources. The team came up with the concept, made the design and modelling decisions, reviewed and ran all code, and checked every cited source. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used.

Team and references

Team CosmoMyszki: Jan Domański (backend developer), Kamila Bąk (frontend developer), Zuzanna Marciniak (UX/UI designer).

All data, sources and software with licenses: https://github.com/MoAI-PL/NASASpaceApps-MoAI#11-references. No NASA logos or branding are used. Every astronaut is synthetic ("Crew Member Alpha, Bravo, Charlie").
